div.head: Chapter 10
div.p: The second part, namely: that if those peoples, after the faith has been preached to them and they have received it, do not wish to pay the expenses that the kings shall have incurred in this, they may not be compelled to pay nor to contribute any part of those expenses. This is proved by many reasons. The first, because by precept of Christ, we are bound to give freely, just as we freely received the faith. Matthew 10: "The worker is worthy of his food," that is, according to Jerome, only this: "Take what is necessary for your clothing and sustenance."

The second, because upon the supreme pastor of the universal Church, and upon the others upon whom by office it falls, or upon those to whom he entrusts it, there falls by divine precept given absolutely by Christ the duty to ensure and command that the Gospel be preached to all peoples, throughout the whole world, without distinction or mention or any condition of price or of expenses. For when preaching is commanded, it is also commanded that the costs and expenses be borne, as has been said. So Christ commanded: Mark, last chapter: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature," et Matthew, last chapter: "Go and teach all nations, etc." And Saint Paul, 1 Corinthians 9, recognizing that it was a precept for him, said: "For if I preach the Gospel, I have no cause for boasting, for necessity is laid upon me," as if to say: "little thanks to me if I fulfill it, for I am bound to it under pain of eternal damnation by divine precept," for which reason what follows: "Woe to me if I preach not the Gospel!" — that is, according to the Gloss and Saint Thomas: my heavenly glory would surely be forfeited if I preached in order to receive payment, etc. The third, because the preaching of the faith, by divine ordination, is owed without any distinction to all the peoples of the world, because that is owed to each one which is ordained for him according to the order of divine wisdom, as Saint Thomas, 1 q. 2 a. 1 ad 3, teaches. And therefore, in paying what he owes, a man is not permitted to demand expenses from the creditor. For the Supreme Pontiff and the other ministers of the Church, as debtors bound to convert the peoples — who in this respect are their creditors — as that passage of Saint Paul, Romans 1 says: "To Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to the unwise, I am a debtor; so, as much as in me is, I am ready to preach the Gospel to you also who are at Rome." Saint Bernard, book 3, De consideratione, to Pope Eugenius: "If then you recognize that you are not a lord but a debtor to the wise and the unwise, you must take the greatest care and apply all vigilance to considering how those who are not wise may become so and how those who are wise may not fall into folly. You are therefore also a debtor to unbelievers, both Jews and Greeks and gentiles. It is therefore right that you devote all the diligence you can to the end that unbelievers be converted to the faith, and those already converted do not turn away from it, etc." Thus far Bernard.

The fourth, because if we were to ask of the unbelieving hearers of the Gospel their expenses or any other thing at a price, they would think we were selling them the Gospel and that we preached it to them for gain and profit, and not to convert them to Christ and save their souls. So says Saint Jerome on Saint Matthew: if the apostles received gold and silver, they would seem to be preaching not for the salvation of men but for profit.
And the gloss on that passage of 2 Corinthians 12, "I seek not yours but you," says: he seeks not gifts or donations, but fruit, lest he appear to be a vendor of the Gospel.

Christ therefore permitted his preachers only to receive and take food from those to whom they preached the Gospel. And this the apostle himself shows: "Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content," 1 Corinthians 6. And to give more than this, Christ did not bind those to whom the faith is preached and who receive it. And even as regards this food, if such persons are unwilling to give it, he imposed no bodily or temporal penalties; just as he imposed no penalties in this world upon those who were unwilling to receive the preachers of the Gospel, or to receive them or hear them; rather the punishment and chastisement of that sin he reserved for himself on the day of final judgment: "And whoever will not receive you or hear your words, go out of that house or city and shake off the dust from your feet. Truly I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city." Matthew 10. "And whoever does not believe shall be condemned." By this authority, those who presume to affirm that if unbelievers do not receive the preachers or are unwilling to hear them, they can be forced to do so by Catholics, ought to put their finger to their lips; for these are nothing but pretexts to scandalize and rob the unbelievers, to usurp their dominions, and to ensure that they never come to the faith, as appears from what has been said. Returning to the subject: Saint Paul did not excommunicate the Corinthians, as he could have, after they had received the faith, nor did he thunder any other temporal penalty against those who out of their own greed would not and did not provide food to him and his companions. He did no more than

reproach them as ungrateful, saying: "Because I preached the Gospel of God to you freely, I robbed other churches, receiving wages, that is, food, for my ministry to you. And when I was with you and in need, I was not a burden to anyone; for what I lacked, the brethren supplied who came from Macedonia. And in all things I kept and will keep myself from being a burden to you, etc." At times he worked with his own hands to buy food for himself and for those who went with him and helped him. Being at Miletus, he said to those he had preached to: "Silver or gold or clothing I coveted from no one, as you yourselves know. For what was needed for me and for those who are with me, these hands provided. In all things I have shown you that by so laboring it is necessary to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, who said: it is more blessed to give than to receive." Acts 20. What has been said is not hindered by the fact that not only by divine law, as has appeared, but also by natural law, the apostle proves that those who preach and serve the Gospel are owed what is necessary: "For no one serves as a soldier at his own expense," 1 Corinthians 9. For to whoever serves the common good, natural reason dictates that the necessities of life are owed. All of which is true; therefore, those who have received the faith may be compelled to fulfill in this case the debt they owe to the preachers, by natural and divine law, etc. To which we respond that unbelievers, even after their conversion, if out of their own greed or some other irrational motive they are unwilling to give what is necessary to the very persons who preached or preach to them, sin gravely, not only in acting as ingrates; but that sin is not punishable by men in this life with spiritual or temporal penalty, but in the other world, whose punishment Christ reserved for himself, as has been seen. For although this obligation is one of natural law, it is nonetheless like the antidotal obligation that arises from that natural equity which dictates that we give thanks and do good to those who do good to us; of which the civil lawyers treat in the L. sed in lege, § consuluit, ff. De petitione hereditatis, et in c. cum in officiis, de testamentis; but from it no action arises or is available: nec potest deduci in compensationem, L. hoc iure, penúlt., De donationibus. And therefore no one can be compelled to pay the debt which he has contracted through this obligation, just as he cannot be compelled to give alms to a neighboring pauper living in extreme need, and so with the other works of mercy, to which every man is nonetheless bound by natural and divine law, under pain of mortal sin and eternal damnation, as appears in Matthew 25: "For I was hungry and you gave me no food, etc." But no spiritual or temporal judge has power to punish or constrain such persons. And this because Christ reserved the punishment of it for himself, leaving such works to the freedom of each person and to their free will. In the same way, Christ left it to the will of those who would hear or not hear the faith willingly, and would receive or not receive it, to maintain and provide to the preachers what is necessary for their life. Let this be notably said: "those who are unwilling to give to the very persons who preach what is necessary"; for to more than what those very persons strictly require they are not bound, because it is to be understood that everything else demanded of them for superfluities, such as building sumptuous churches or monasteries and other excesses that under pretexts and the guise of preaching are demanded of them and were or are made to be done: all of this is robbery, and they must render a strict account to God for it. All of this is proved by that limited license which Christ gave: "The worker is worthy of his food," and "eat what is set before you," Luke 10. He did not say: "you shall take their superfluous food, or their necessary food, or anything beyond it," but rather: "Eat what they give you, and if they give you nothing, go elsewhere, for in the end I have provided that none of the things necessary to you shall be lacking."

And so it appears that the unbelievers may not be compelled, nor even after becoming Christians, to pay the costs that shall be incurred to go and preach to them, but that the kings of Castile took charge, as regards the Indies, of bringing about their conversion, and the pope imposed a precept upon them to this end, without thereby extracting a single maravedí from them by force. And the same reasoning applies to any other public or private person to whom the vicar of Christ might entrust this care and office in general or in particular, who would be bound to bear the costs without seeking any recompense from them, at least without forcing them to it; for it is written, Ecclesiasticus 17: "God commanded each one concerning his neighbor," and Matthew 7: "Whatever you wish men to do to you, do also to them."
